answers.java_tx_design: Our wallet-service wraps the payout write in one transaction; a senior engineer, Priya, set that boundary before I joined. I added a new column and a read method inside it last year, under her review. I haven't had to move a boundary myself. When I asked why it's structured that way, she said it keeps balance updates atomic with the payout row, and I've taken that as correct rather than testing it myself.
answers.java_ops: Our SRE team owns GC tuning and Kubernetes config for wallet-service; I've sat in on two incident calls where they adjusted heap size, but I didn't do the diagnosis myself. Once I bumped a connection pool from 10 to 20 on Priya's instruction after a dashboard she was watching showed wait times climbing. I couldn't tell you the exact numbers behind that call, just that it worked.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust in production, just Rustlings exercises this year, maybe 15 hours total. My plan is to finish those, then build a small CLI that parses our payout CSV exports, over the next two months, before touching anything with async. I think ownership will take longest to click. On boundaries, I'd lean on whoever's done a migration before rather than guess.
answers.rust_boundary: Honestly I don't have a real answer here yet. If asked to move part of a ledger write path, I'd want to sit with a senior engineer first and watch what they measure, since I've never made that call myself. My guess is you'd watch latency and error counts, but I'd rather admit I'm guessing than make it sound like experience I have.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't built idempotency handling myself. Our payout retries go through a Kafka consumer with a dedupe table that a senior engineer designed before I joined; I've read the code but never had to design or fix that mechanism, and I've never had a duplicate-payout incident land on my desk to debug.
answers.incident_response: There was a payout duplication incident about a year ago, before I'd been on wallet-service long enough to be on the response. I heard about it in the postmortem doc but wasn't part of triage or the fix. The closest I've come to incident response myself is restarting a stuck consumer once, at a senior's direction.
answers.process_skipping: I haven't been in a situation urgent enough to be tempted to skip review. Our deploy pipeline requires one approval regardless, and I've always waited for it, even when a fix felt obvious. I think skipping would need real, ongoing harm and someone else's sign-off recorded somewhere, not just my own sense that I'm right.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I told my lead the same day I shipped a null-check bug that caused a small spike in failed payout requests, maybe 40 of them, rather than waiting to see if anyone noticed. I've done on-call for about eight months, one week in six, mostly routing pages to a senior since I can't fix most issues alone yet.
answers.evidence_decision: I pushed back once on adding a new wallet-balance cache, saying it could go stale, but I didn't have data, just a hunch, and the team went with it anyway. I didn't build a competing version afterward; I helped implement the agreed cache and watched to see if my worry showed up, which it didn't.
answers.own_contribution: Fair question. In the payout write-path I described, the part that was really mine was adding the new balance column and its read method; Priya designed the transaction boundary and the retry/dedupe table. In a different case, updating our on-call runbook, I wrote the whole document myself but the escalation policy inside it came from my lead.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't personally restored broken production data. There was a missing-journal-entry issue in wallet-service before I joined that a senior fixed with a backfill script; I only know about it from the incident doc, not from doing the work.
answers.java_perf_change: I haven't led a measured performance change myself. I once added an index a senior suggested after she'd already found the slow query in a profiler, and I watched our dashboard latency drop afterward, but the profiling and the decision were hers, not mine.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written enough Rust to have hit a real ownership or lifetime wall yet -- my Rustlings exercises so far have been mostly guided, so the compiler errors get explained by the exercise, not fought through on my own. I expect that's coming once I start the CSV parser project.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have the experience to say much here beyond the general idea that you wouldn't touch something stable and rarely changed. I haven't held back a rewrite urge myself, since I've never proposed one; I'd want to learn from someone who has before I'd trust my own judgment on it.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased down a reconciliation mismatch myself. I know we run a nightly job that compares wallet balances to the payment processor's records, and I've seen its output in Slack, but investigating a mismatch has always gone to a senior engineer, not to me.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been tempted to check production balances directly, mostly because I've never had a case I couldn't verify in staging. If I hit one, I'd ask a senior how they've verified things that don't reproduce in test, since I don't have my own method for that yet.
